course.title: Cybersecurity & Digital Safety
course.description: Practical digital safety for everyday users and small organisations: devices, privacy, accounts, phishing, mobile money and incident response. Beginner to competent defender of your own digital life and workplace.

lessons.title: Lesson 1.1: How digital systems are attacked
lessons.description: Common goals and methods of attackers.
lessons.notesHtml:
Aim

Explain common attacker goals (money, data, disruption) and high-level methods.

lessons.title: Lesson 1.2: Devices, networks and updates
lessons.description: Keep systems patched and networks safer.
lessons.notesHtml:
Aim

Apply update discipline and basic network hygiene on phones and computers.

lessons.title: Lesson 1.3: Staying secure day to day
lessons.notesHtml:
Aim

Adopt a short daily/weekly security checklist.

lessons.title: Module 1 review and assessment
lessons.notesHtml:
Module 1 review and assessment

10 questions. Pass mark 70 %.
lessons.quiz:
Q: Common attacker goals include:
Helping users only
*Money, data theft, disruption or access for further attacks
Improving software quality
Only testing systems legally
explain: Adversarial goals.
level: 1

Q: Software updates matter because:
They only change colours
*They often fix known security vulnerabilities
They always slow devices
They are optional for security
explain: Patches close holes.
level: 1

Q: Using untrusted public Wi-Fi for sensitive tasks without protection is:
Always safe
*Risky because traffic may be intercepted
Required
Only a problem for images
explain: Network interception risk.
level: 1

Q: A daily security habit might include:
Sharing passwords
*Checking for unexpected login alerts and keeping devices locked
Disabling all updates
Clicking every link
explain: Awareness + lock screens.
level: 1

Q: Malware is:
Always visible
*Software designed to harm, spy or exploit systems
Only a Windows problem
Harmless by definition
explain: Malicious software.
level: 1

Q: Reducing the number of apps with broad permissions:
Increases risk
*Reduces the damage if one app is compromised
Has no effect
Is impossible on phones
explain: Least privilege.
level: 2

Q: Backups help security by:
Preventing all attacks
*Enabling recovery after ransomware or device loss
Replacing passwords
Stopping phishing
explain: Recovery capability.
level: 2

Q: Physical security of devices matters because:
Thieves never want phones
*Lost or stolen devices can expose accounts and data
Only servers need physical security
Locks are cosmetic
explain: Physical access is powerful.
level: 1

Q: Attackers often prefer:
Hard targets only
*Easy targets with valuable data or money
Only government systems
Systems with perfect security
explain: Opportunistic targeting.
level: 2

Q: The foundation of personal cyber safety is:
Buying every product advertised
*Good habits: updates, strong authentication, careful clicking, backups
Never using the internet
Only antivirus with no other habits
explain: Habits compound.
level: 1

lessons.title: Lesson 2.1: Your digital footprint
lessons.description: What you leave behind and who can see it.
lessons.notesHtml:
Aim

Audit your own public footprint and reduce unnecessary exposure.

lessons.title: Lesson 2.2: Privacy settings and sharing
lessons.description: Control what apps and platforms collect.
lessons.notesHtml:
Aim

Adjust key privacy settings on phone and major accounts.

lessons.title: Lesson 2.3: Safe use of social media
lessons.notesHtml:
Aim

Apply practical rules for what not to post and how to handle suspicious contacts.

lessons.title: Module 2 review and assessment
lessons.notesHtml:
Module 2 review and assessment

10 questions. Pass mark 70 %.
lessons.quiz:
Q: Digital footprint includes:
Only your private notes
*Public posts, photos, comments, and data shared with services
Only your password
Nothing permanent
explain: Persistent traces.
level: 1

Q: Oversharing location and routines can:
Improve privacy
*Help criminals plan theft or scams
Only help friends
Have no risk
explain: Predictability aids attackers.
level: 1

Q: Reviewing app permissions helps:
Grant every permission always
*Limit data access to what is necessary
Slow the phone only
Delete the app store
explain: Least privilege for apps.
level: 1

Q: Privacy settings should be reviewed:
Never after signup
*Periodically and after major app updates
Only once in a lifetime
Only by the platform
explain: Defaults and changes drift.
level: 2

Q: Tagging strangers in photos can:
Always be safe
*Expose people’s identities and locations without consent
Improve security
Delete metadata
explain: Consent and exposure.
level: 2

Q: A practical privacy habit is:
Using the same personal details everywhere unnecessarily
*Minimising what you share and with whom
Posting ID documents for verification on social media
Ignoring all settings
explain: Minimisation.
level: 1

Q: Scammers use public information to:
Help you
*Craft believable phishing and social-engineering attacks
Improve your credit score
Update your software
explain: OSINT for scams.
level: 1

Q: Separating work and personal accounts can:
Increase confusion only
*Limit blast radius if one account is compromised
Have no security benefit
Be impossible
explain: Containment.
level: 2

Q: Accepting unknown friend requests from attractive profiles is:
Always wise
*A common social-engineering vector
Required for networking
Risk-free
explain: Fake profiles are common.
level: 1

Q: The goal of privacy practice is:
Hiding from all friends
*Controlling who can access your information and reducing unnecessary risk
Avoiding all technology
Making accounts unusable
explain: Control + risk reduction.
level: 1

lessons.title: Lesson 3.1: Strong passwords and password managers
lessons.notesHtml:
Aim

Adopt a password manager and unique strong passwords for important accounts.

lessons.title: Lesson 3.2: Two-step verification
lessons.notesHtml:
Aim

Enable multi-factor authentication on critical accounts and understand backup codes.

lessons.title: Lesson 3.3: Recovering a compromised account
lessons.notesHtml:
Aim

Follow a practical response checklist if an account is taken over.

lessons.title: Module 3 review and assessment
lessons.notesHtml:
Module 3 review and assessment

10 questions. Pass mark 70 %.
lessons.quiz:
Q: Reusing the same password across sites is:
Best practice
*Dangerous because one breach unlocks many accounts
Required by banks
Only a problem for email
explain: Credential stuffing risk.
level: 1

Q: A password manager helps by:
Sharing all passwords publicly
*Storing unique strong passwords and filling them safely
Replacing MFA
Making passwords shorter
explain: Unique secrets at scale.
level: 1

Q: Multi-factor authentication (MFA) adds:
Only inconvenience
*A second proof of identity beyond the password
A way to avoid passwords forever without risk
Nothing useful
explain: Second factor.
level: 1

Q: Backup codes for MFA should be:
Posted on social media
*Stored securely offline or in a safe place
Shared with colleagues casually
Ignored
explain: Recovery when the second factor is lost.
level: 2

Q: If you suspect account compromise you should:
Do nothing
*Change password, review sessions/devices, enable MFA, and check recovery settings
Only post about it
Share the password to get help from strangers
explain: Contain and harden.
level: 1

Q: SMS-based codes are:
Perfectly secure always
*Better than passwords alone but weaker than app-based or hardware factors against some attacks
Useless
The only form of MFA
explain: Better than nothing; not the strongest.
level: 2

Q: Password length and uniqueness matter more than:
Using the same short password everywhere
*Complex rules on a short reused password
Never changing breached passwords
Writing passwords on the monitor
explain: Length + uniqueness win.
level: 2

Q: Reviewing active sessions helps you:
Increase open sessions
*Spot and revoke unknown logins
Share access widely
Disable MFA
explain: Session hygiene.
level: 1

Q: Recovery email and phone numbers should be:
Outdated
*Current and themselves well protected
Public
The same as the account password
explain: Recovery path security.
level: 1

Q: The combination that stops most account takeovers is:
A short shared password only
*Unique strong password + MFA + careful recovery settings
No password
Only security questions from public data
explain: Layered account defence.
level: 1

modules.title: Module 4: Phishing and cyber threats
modules.description: Spot scams, malware and mobile-money fraud.

lessons.title: Lesson 4.1: Spotting phishing and scams
lessons.notesHtml:
Aim

Identify common phishing cues and verify unexpected requests out-of-band.

lessons.title: Lesson 4.2: Malware, ransomware and fraud
lessons.description: What they are and how to reduce exposure.
lessons.notesHtml:
Aim

Explain ransomware and practical defences including backups and careful downloads.

lessons.title: Lesson 4.3: Mobile money and online safety
lessons.notesHtml:
Aim

Apply mobile-money safety rules and recognise common local scam patterns.

lessons.title: Module 4 review and assessment
lessons.notesHtml:
Module 4 review and assessment

10 questions. Pass mark 70 %.
lessons.quiz:
Q: Phishing aims to:
Improve your security
*Trick you into revealing secrets or installing malware
Update your software safely
Only send newsletters
explain: Deceptive credential or malware delivery.
level: 1

Q: Unexpected urgent requests for money or codes should be:
Obeyed immediately
*Verified through a separate trusted channel
Forwarded to all contacts
Ignored forever without checking
explain: Out-of-band verification.
level: 1

Q: Ransomware typically:
Improves file organisation
*Encrypts files and demands payment for recovery
Only affects paper documents
Is harmless
explain: Extortion via encryption.
level: 1

Q: Offline or versioned backups help against ransomware by:
Preventing all infections
*Allowing restoration without paying the attacker
Sharing files publicly
Replacing antivirus
explain: Recovery option.
level: 1

Q: Mobile-money PIN should be:
Shared with helpful callers
*Kept private; never typed when someone is “guiding” you
The same as your birthday
Written on the phone case
explain: PIN secrecy.
level: 1

Q: A common scam pattern is:
Official support that never asks for secrets
*Impersonation of support, banks or relatives plus urgency
Slow careful verification
Written contracts only
explain: Impersonation + urgency.
level: 1

Q: Clicking links in unexpected messages is:
Always safe if the logo looks right
*Risky; prefer navigating to sites directly via known bookmarks
Required for updates
Only dangerous on computers
explain: Direct navigation is safer.
level: 2

Q: If you sent money to a scammer you should:
Send more to recover it
*Stop further contact, document everything, and report to the provider and relevant authorities
Only wait
Share your ID to get a refund from the scammer
explain: Contain and report.
level: 2

Q: Attachment risk is higher when:
The sender is expected and the file type matches the context
*The message is unexpected and urges you to open a document or enable macros
You scanned the file
The file is a plain text note from a known colleague
explain: Unexpected + macros = danger.
level: 2

Q: Healthy scepticism toward unexpected digital requests is:
Paranoia
*A core security skill
Unnecessary with antivirus
Only for IT staff
explain: Human layer of defence.
level: 1

modules.title: Module 5: Information protection
modules.description: Files, work security and incident response.

lessons.title: Lesson 5.1: Protecting files and backups
lessons.notesHtml:
Aim

Apply practical file protection and a workable backup routine.

lessons.title: Lesson 5.2: Security at work
lessons.notesHtml:
Aim

Follow workplace security rules and report issues promptly.

lessons.title: Lesson 5.3: Reporting and responding to incidents
lessons.description: What to do when something goes wrong.
lessons.notesHtml:
Aim

Execute a simple personal and workplace incident response sequence.

lessons.title: Module 5 review and assessment
lessons.notesHtml:
Module 5 review and assessment

10 questions. Pass mark 70 %.
lessons.quiz:
Q: Good backups are:
Only in the same folder as the originals
*Separate, tested, and sufficiently frequent for your risk
Never tested
Only in email
explain: Separate + tested.
level: 1

Q: Encrypting sensitive files helps when:
Devices are lost or stolen
*Devices or drives are lost, stolen or improperly accessed
You want slower performance only
Sharing widely without controls
explain: Confidentiality at rest.
level: 1

Q: Workplace security is:
Only the IT department’s job
*A shared responsibility; individuals must follow policy and report issues
Optional for senior staff
Only about physical doors
explain: Shared responsibility.
level: 1

Q: Reporting incidents early helps:
Create panic only
*Limit damage and speed recovery
Guarantee no consequences ever
Replace all controls
explain: Time matters.
level: 1

Q: A simple incident response sequence includes:
Deleting all evidence first
*Contain, preserve evidence where appropriate, eradicate, recover, and learn
Only rebooting
Ignoring it
explain: Structured response.
level: 2

Q: Access to shared drives should follow:
Everyone gets full access
*Need-to-know and least privilege
No access controls
Only alphabetical order
explain: Least privilege.
level: 2

Q: Testing a restore from backup is important because:
Backups never fail
*Untested backups often fail when needed
It is illegal
It replaces primary storage
explain: Test restores.
level: 1

Q: Suspicious activity on a work account should be:
Hidden to avoid blame
*Reported according to policy immediately
Discussed only on social media
Ignored if small
explain: Prompt reporting.
level: 1

Q: After an incident, learning reviews help:
Blame individuals only
*Improve controls and reduce repeat events
Avoid all documentation
Punish reporters
explain: Systemic improvement.
level: 2

Q: The overall aim of this course is to help you:
Fear all technology
*Practise realistic digital safety habits that protect you, your money and your organisation
Become a professional hacker overnight
Avoid all online services
explain: Practical resilient habits.
level: 1
